title: Source-grounded verification of the Gandhara halo-synthesis [R-Anker] claim in OTA-FND-0022 ('griechischer Nimbus / zoroastrische Khvarenah / buddhistische Prabha als ein ikonographisches System') against the art-historical literature
question: (a) Is the halo/nimbus in Buddhist art a genuine syncretism of Hellenistic-Greek radiate iconography (Helios/Apollo), Zoroastrian khvarenah (divine glory/light) and Indic concepts (prabha, ushnisha, aura), and was Gandhara (present-day Pakistan/Afghanistan, Kushan-era Greco-Buddhist art) the first 1st-5th century CE site where these three fused into a single iconographic system — or do the primary art-historical sources trace the Buddhist halo to a different origin (Greco-Roman import vs. indigenous Indian tradition, e.g. Surya iconography) and date its first appearance differently? (b) What do the earliest attested Gandharan halos (Bimaran casket, early Bodhisattva/Buddha reliefs, stucco heads) actually show, and which primary/publication evidence dates them? (c) How is Avestan xvarənah/khvarenah defined in the primary Zoroastrian texts, and is the 'glory manifested as halo' reading defensible in the secondary literature? (d) Is the philological record consistent with the doc's name-connection between gandhaka (Sanskrit 'sulphur', from gandha 'smell') and Gandhara (region name etymology)? (e) Which specific claims of the referenced halo-diffusion map (OTA-CUL-0015, Heiligenschein-Straße; routes from Iran/Gandhara to Rome, China, Southeast Asia) rest on this anchor, and where does the literature conflict with the stated 1st-5th century timing or the claimed tripartite synthesis?
why_now: The GANDHAKA title-genesis and the entire referenced halo-iconography architecture of OTA-CUL-0015 (Heiligenschein-Straße, halo diffusion routes) rest on this single [R-Anker] claim. It has never been externally audited: no prior OTA research topic covers Gandharan art or halo iconography, and the claim bundles three distinct scholarly traditions (Hellenistic, Zoroastrian, Buddhist) whose synthesis is contested in art history — so an anchor check can materially affect how the archive labels the title genesis and the CUL-0015 route map.
real_world_anchor: The historical claim that Gandhara (present-day Pakistan/Afghanistan) was the 1st-5th century CE synthesis node where Greek nimbus iconography, Zoroastrian khvarenah, and Buddhist prabha first fused into a single halo iconographic system.
novelty_reason: No prior OTA research topic covers Gandharan art or halo iconography; the closest neighbor, RES-20260823-7E477B58, addresses the Sanxingdui/Sea Peoples line of OTA-CUL-0015, not its Gandhara halo-synthesis claim. This gap is not a rephrase or broadening of any listed topic.
